note: Dictating an emergency department note on a 44-year-old male who presents with sudden severe headache. He states it began about two hours ago while he was lifting weights at the gym, reached full intensity within seconds, and is the worst headache of his life, rated nine out of ten, located at the back of the head. He has some nausea but no vomiting, no fever, no neck stiffness, no vision changes, no weakness or numbness, and no head injury. He has no chronic medical conditions and takes no regular medications. Vital signs on arrival blood pressure 148/88, heart rate 82, temperature 98.4 F, oxygen saturation 99% on room air. On exam he is uncomfortable but alert and oriented, neck is supple, cranial nerves are intact, strength and sensation are normal, gait is normal, no papilledema. We obtained a noncontrast CT of the head which showed no hemorrhage, and a CT angiogram of the head and neck which showed no aneurysm and no dissection. Since the CT was done within six hours of onset and read as normal, subarachnoid hemorrhage is effectively ruled out and no lumbar puncture is needed. Impression is primary exertional headache, correction, primary thunderclap headache triggered by exertion. He received acetaminophen 1000 mg by mouth and metoclopramide 10 mg IV and his pain improved to three out of ten. He will be discharged home with acetaminophen 1000 mg every 6 hours as needed, avoid heavy lifting for one week, follow up with primary care in one week and with neurology if the headache recurs, and return immediately for worsening headache, vomiting, confusion, weakness, or fever.
summary: A 44-year-old male presented to the emergency department with a sudden severe headache that began about two hours earlier while lifting weights. He reported nausea but denied vomiting, fever, neck stiffness, vision changes, weakness, and numbness, and his neurologic exam was normal. Noncontrast head CT and CT angiogram of the head and neck showed no hemorrhage, aneurysm, or dissection. The impression was primary thunderclap headache triggered by exertion, and pain improved to three out of ten after acetaminophen and metoclopramide. He was discharged on acetaminophen as needed with activity restriction, primary care and neurology follow-up, and return precautions.

note:
Doctor: Hi, come on in. So I hear this little guy has been really itchy. What's been going on?
Family member: Yes, he's had eczema since he was a baby, but this past week it's gotten so much worse. He scratches all night long and barely sleeps, and now some spots on his arms are oozing and crusty.
Doctor: Okay, so we have a 3-year-old male with known atopic dermatitis and a flare. Any fever?
Family member: No fever. No vomiting or diarrhea either, he's eating and drinking fine.
Doctor: Good. Any trouble breathing or wheezing?
Family member: No trouble breathing, no wheezing. He doesn't have asthma or any food allergies.
Doctor: Anything new at home, like soaps, pets, or foods?
Family member: We changed laundry detergent about two weeks ago. Nothing else new.
Doctor: And what have you been putting on his skin?
Family member: Hydrocortisone 1% cream, once or twice a day, plus a lotion after baths. It doesn't seem to help anymore.
Doctor: Alright, let's take a look. His temperature is 98.7, heart rate 104, respiratory rate 22, oxygen saturation 99% on room air, and he weighs about 15 kilos. On exam there are dry, red, scaly patches on both cheeks, the inner elbows, and behind the knees, with lots of scratch marks. On the right forearm and the chin there are honey-colored crusts. Lungs are clear and there are no swollen lymph nodes. I did a skin scraping from one scaly patch for a KOH prep, and it is negative for fungus, so this is not ringworm.
Family member: Okay, so what is it then?
Doctor: This is an atopic dermatitis flare with a secondary bacterial skin infection called impetigo on the forearm and chin. The hydrocortisone 1% is just too weak for his body. So I'm going to stop it on his body and start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice a day to the red patches on the body, arms, and legs for up to two weeks, but not on the face. You can keep using the hydrocortisone 1% cream on his face. For the crusted spots I'm starting mupirocin 2% ointment, a thin layer three times a day for seven days.
Family member: Should we change anything with his baths?
Doctor: Short lukewarm baths, then put a thick moisturizer on within a few minutes, and go back to a fragrance-free detergent. Keep his nails trimmed short. I'd like him back with his pediatrician in one week, and come back sooner if he gets a fever, the redness spreads, or you see painful blisters.
Family member: Got it, thank you.
summary: A 3-year-old male presented to urgent care with a week-long flare of his known atopic dermatitis with severe itching, poor sleep, and oozing, crusted spots on the arms. Examination showed dry, red, scaly patches with scratch marks and honey-colored crusts on the right forearm and chin, and a KOH prep from a scaly patch was negative for fungus. The diagnosis was an atopic dermatitis flare with secondary impetigo. Hydrocortisone 1% was stopped on the body but continued on the face, triamcinolone 0.1% ointment and mupirocin 2% ointment were started, and pediatrician follow-up in one week was advised.

70-year-old male, geriatrics clinic f/u for memory concerns.

PMH: HTN, T2DM, HLD.
Meds: metformin 500 mg BID, Januvia 100 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily. NKDA.

VS: BP 152/88, HR 74, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA, Wt 82 kg.
Exam: A&O x3, MoCA 22/30 (lost pts on delayed recall + visuospatial/clock), CN intact, no tremor or rigidity, gait normal, no focal deficits.
Labs: A1c 8.4%, Cr 1.1, eGFR 68, TSH 2.4, B12 520.

Impression: MCI, likely amnestic type. HTN and T2DM above goal, partly from cost-related non-adherence.

- no cholinesterase inhibitor for now
- MRI brain w/o contrast, neuropsych testing referral
- stop Januvia (cost). Increase metformin to 1000 mg BID (eGFR OK)

- atorvastatin 40 mg daily, take every day; switch to 90-day generic supply

note:
Telehealth visit, telephone (audio only). Rheumatology follow-up for psoriatic arthritis. The patient confirmed her identity verbally and consented to a phone visit; she was at home during the call.

History as reported by the patient: a 67-year-old female with psoriatic arthritis for 6 years. She reports ongoing morning stiffness lasting about an hour, pain and swelling in the right knee and left wrist, and a swollen left second toe. Scalp plaques are stable. She has fatigue. She denies fever, eye redness or pain, back pain, mouth ulcers, diarrhea, chest pain, new cough, and shortness of breath. She smokes about 10 cigarettes a day and has smoked for 40 years; she is not ready to quit but is willing to talk about it.

Current medications are methotrexate 15 mg weekly, folic acid 1 mg daily, and naproxen 500 mg twice daily. She reports taking them correctly and has missed no methotrexate doses.

Home measurements: BP 132/80 and pulse 76 on her home cuff.

Limited exam: no video was available, so no physical exam was performed. She speaks in full sentences without audible shortness of breath.

Results reviewed: labs from last week show CRP 14 mg/L and ESR 36, with ALT 24, Hgb 12.9, WBC 6.8, and Cr 0.8. QuantiFERON-TB and hepatitis B surface antigen were both negative.

Impression: psoriatic arthritis with persistent moderate disease activity despite methotrexate, and current tobacco use.

Next steps: start adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks. Continue methotrexate 15 mg weekly and folic acid 1 mg daily. Reduce naproxen to 500 mg as needed instead of twice daily. We discussed that smoking can blunt the response to biologic therapy, and she agreed to start a nicotine patch 14 mg daily. X-rays of the hands and feet are ordered. Repeat CBC, creatinine, and ALT in 4 weeks. Telephone follow-up in 6 weeks; she should call sooner for fever, signs of infection, or a flare.

Adalimumab was started, naproxen was reduced to as needed, a nicotine patch was started, and hand and foot X-rays and repeat labs were ordered.

note:
Doctor: Hi there, come on in. I hear he's got a barky cough. Tell me what's been going on.
Family member: Yes, it started with a runny nose two days ago, and then tonight he woke up with this awful barking cough and a noisy sound when he breathes in. It really scared me.
Doctor: I'm sure it did. So this is a 5-year-old male with a barky cough since last night. Has he had a fever?
Family member: He felt warm, I think around 100, so I gave him children's acetaminophen about two hours ago.
Doctor: Okay. Any drooling or trouble swallowing?
Family member: No drooling, and he's been drinking fine.
Doctor: Any chance he swallowed or choked on something, like a small toy or food?
Family member: No, nothing like that. No vomiting either, and no rash.
Doctor: Has he had croup before, or any asthma?
Family member: Never croup, and no asthma. His shots are up to date and he has no medicine allergies.
Doctor: Good. Did you give him any cough syrup?
Family member: Yes, a dose of an over-the-counter cough syrup last night, but it didn't do anything.
Doctor: Okay, let's check him. His temperature is 100.4, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, and he weighs 18 kilos. He's sitting comfortably in your lap. He has that barking cough, and when he gets upset I hear some inspiratory stridor, but at rest there is no stridor and no retractions. His throat is mildly red, ears are clear, and the lungs have good air movement with no wheezing. I also did a rapid flu and COVID swab and both are negative.
Family member: So what is it?
Doctor: This is croup, a viral infection that swells the area just below the vocal cords. Because he has stridor when he's upset, I'm going to give him dexamethasone 10 mg by mouth right now, one single dose, which helps the swelling. We'll watch him here for about an hour. Stop the cough syrup, it doesn't help croup. For fever or discomfort you can give acetaminophen 270 mg every 6 hours as needed.
Family member: Is it okay to go home after that?
Doctor: If he stays comfortable with no stridor at rest during the observation, yes. Keep him calm, and a steamy bathroom or cool night air can help if he gets noisy. Call his pediatrician tomorrow for a recheck, and come back right away or call 911 if you hear stridor at rest, he's drooling, he's working hard to breathe, or his lips look blue.
Family member: Okay, thank you.
summary: A 5-year-old male presented to urgent care with a runny nose for two days followed by a barking cough and noisy breathing that began the night before. On exam his temperature was 100.4, oxygen saturation was 97% on room air, and he had inspiratory stridor only when upset, with no stridor at rest, no retractions, and no wheezing. A rapid flu and COVID swab was negative. The diagnosis was croup, and he received a single oral dose of dexamethasone with observation in clinic, was told to stop cough syrup, and was given acetaminophen as needed with return precautions and pediatrician follow-up.

No prior croup and no asthma; vaccines up to date; no medicine allergies. Was given an over-the-counter cough syrup last night without benefit.
soap.objective: Temperature 100.4, heart rate 112, respiratory rate 26, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, weight 18 kilos. Sitting comfortably; barking cough with some inspiratory stridor when upset but no stridor at rest and no retractions. Throat mildly red, ears clear, lungs with good air movement and no wheezing. Rapid flu and COVID swab negative.
plan: Dexamethasone 10 mg by mouth as a single dose in clinic
Observe in clinic for about an hour and discharge home if comfortable with no stridor at rest
Stop the cough syrup
Acetaminophen 270 mg every 6 hours as needed for fever or discomfort
Keep him calm; steamy bathroom or cool night air if noisy
Pediatrician recheck tomorrow; return or call 911 for stridor at rest, drooling, hard work of breathing, or blue lips

Rash appeared 3 days later, now ~12 cm and growing, nontender, mildly warm. Mild fatigue, HA, and myalgias x 2 days. No fever, no neck stiffness, no facial droop, no joint swelling, no palpitations, no syncope, no SOB, no rash elsewhere.

note:
This 33-year-old male with a 15-year history of type 1 diabetes is seen in the combined eye and ear, nose, and throat clinic for his annual diabetic retinopathy screening and for a second concern of chronic nasal congestion. He reports no change in vision, no floaters, no flashes of light, and no eye pain. For the past several months he has had persistent nasal stuffiness, clear post-nasal drip, and frequent sneezing, worse in spring, which he has been treating with oxymetazoline nasal spray nearly every night. He denies sinus pressure, facial pain, nosebleeds, ear pain, and hearing loss.

His medications are insulin glargine 24 units at bedtime and insulin lispro with meals. He has had no hypoglycemic episodes. His most recent hemoglobin A1c, drawn two weeks ago, was 8.1%. Blood pressure today is 124/78 with a heart rate of 70.

On examination, uncorrected distance visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye, with intraocular pressures of 15 and 16 mmHg. Pupils are equal and reactive. After dilation with tropicamide 1%, the dilated fundus examination shows scattered microaneurysms and a few dot hemorrhages in both eyes, with no neovascularization and no vitreous hemorrhage. Optical coherence tomography of the macula shows no macular edema, with a central subfield thickness of 260 microns in each eye. Anterior rhinoscopy shows pale, boggy inferior turbinates with clear rhinorrhea, no polyps, and a midline septum. Ears and oropharynx are normal.

Assessment is mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular edema in both eyes, and allergic rhinitis with rhinitis medicamentosa from overuse of oxymetazoline. He should stop oxymetazoline and start fluticasone nasal spray 50 mcg, two sprays in each nostril once daily. Saline rinses were also recommended. Glycemic control with his primary diabetes team was reinforced, with a goal A1c below 7%. We will repeat the dilated eye exam with macular OCT in 12 months, and he will return to the ENT clinic in 6 weeks to review his nasal symptoms.
summary: A 33-year-old male with a 15-year history of type 1 diabetes was seen for annual diabetic retinopathy screening and chronic nasal congestion. He had no visual symptoms, but nightly oxymetazoline use for months of nasal stuffiness, post-nasal drip, and sneezing. The dilated fundus exam showed scattered microaneurysms and dot hemorrhages in both eyes with no macular edema on OCT, and rhinoscopy showed pale, boggy turbinates without polyps. The assessment was mild nonproliferative diabetic retinopathy without macular edema, allergic rhinitis, and rhinitis medicamentosa. Oxymetazoline was stopped, fluticasone nasal spray was started, and he will repeat the eye exam in 12 months and return to ENT in 6 weeks.

The patient is a 71-year-old male seen in the urology clinic for follow-up of overactive bladder. He reports 10 to 12 voids per day with 2 to 3 episodes of nocturia, strong urgency, and occasional urge incontinence that requires him to wear a pad on outings. He was started on oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily three months ago with only partial relief and has developed bothersome dry mouth and worsening constipation. He denies dysuria, gross hematuria, flank pain, fever, and any sensation of incomplete emptying. His history includes hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg daily, and benign prostatic hyperplasia on tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He drinks four to five cups of coffee a day.

Blood pressure today is 142/84 and heart rate is 72. The abdomen is soft and nontender with no suprapubic fullness. Digital rectal exam shows a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate without nodules. Urinalysis is negative for blood, leukocytes, nitrites, and glucose. Post-void residual by bladder scan is 45 mL. A PSA drawn last month was 1.8 ng/mL. His completed bladder diary was reviewed with him.

Assessment is overactive bladder with an inadequate response to, and side effects from, oxybutynin, in the setting of benign prostatic hyperplasia. His blood pressure is acceptable for beta-3 agonist therapy. I discontinued oxybutynin and started mirabegron 25 mg once daily. Tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily and amlodipine 5 mg daily will continue. We discussed reducing coffee to one cup per day, timed voiding every 3 hours, and pelvic floor exercises. He will have his blood pressure rechecked in 4 weeks and return in 8 weeks to assess his response, with the option of increasing mirabegron to 50 mg if needed.

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. I understand you've been having back and leg pain. Tell me what's been going on.
Patient: Yeah, my lower back started hurting about ten days ago, and now there's this pain that runs down my right leg into my foot. It's no big deal, I can manage.
Family member: It is a big deal. I'm his wife. He hasn't slept through the night in a week, he's been limping, and he can barely get out of his chair.
Doctor: Okay, thank you for coming with him. So this is a 52-year-old male with right-sided low back pain radiating down the leg for ten days. Did anything trigger it?
Patient: I was moving boxes in the garage. I felt a pull when I lifted one.
Doctor: Is it worse with any position?
Patient: Sitting and coughing. Bending forward is bad too. Walking around is a little better.
Doctor: Any numbness or tingling?
Patient: A little tingling on top of my foot, by the big toe.
Doctor: Any trouble controlling your bladder or bowels, numbness in the groin or inner thighs, or trouble passing urine?
Patient: No, nothing like that.
Doctor: Any fever, chills, or weight loss you can't explain? Any history of cancer?
Patient: No fever, no weight loss, no cancer.
Family member: And he hasn't fallen, but his right foot kind of catches when he walks.
Doctor: Alright. I see in your chart type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux, is that right?
Patient: Yes, that's right.
Doctor: What are you taking for the pain?
Patient: Just some ibuprofen, 200 mg, maybe once or twice a day.
Family member: That's not right. He's been taking his old 800 mg ibuprofen tablets from his knee surgery, three times a day, for the past week. I counted them.
Patient: Okay, okay, she's right. It's the 800 mg tablets, three times a day.
Doctor: Thank you for clearing that up. What are your other medications?
Patient: I take metformin 500 mg twice a day, lisinopril 20 mg once a day, atorvastatin 40 mg at night, and omeprazole 20 mg in the morning for the reflux. My regular doctor also started gabapentin 300 mg at bedtime four days ago, but it hasn't done much.
Family member: His metformin was bumped up to 1000 mg twice a day last month, so that's the dose now.
Patient: Oh right, 1000 mg twice a day. I forgot.
Doctor: Good. Any allergies to medicines?
Patient: No.
Doctor: Alright. His blood pressure is 146/88, heart rate 84, temperature 98.2, oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He weighs 112 kilos, BMI 35. A fingerstick glucose is 212. On exam, there's no midline spinal tenderness, but there's mild paraspinal muscle spasm on the right. Straight leg raise on the right reproduces the pain down the leg at about 40 degrees, and the left is negative. Strength is 5 out of 5 everywhere except the right big toe extension, which is 4 out of 5. Sensation is decreased over the top of the right foot. Knee and ankle reflexes are 2+ and symmetric. He has an antalgic gait but can walk on his heels and toes. I got a lumbar X-ray here and it shows mild disc space narrowing at L4-L5 and L5-S1, no fracture, and no spondylolisthesis. His creatinine from his regular doctor last month was 0.9 with an eGFR of 88, and his A1c was 8.3%.
Family member: So what does that mean?
Doctor: This looks like a right L5 lumbar radiculopathy, most likely from a disc herniation at L4-L5 pressing on the nerve root, and there are no red flags like cauda equina symptoms. Because of his diabetes, his kidneys, the reflux, and the lisinopril and metformin, I want him to stop the ibuprofen completely. High-dose NSAIDs can hurt the kidneys and the stomach. Start acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours on a schedule. Increase the gabapentin from 300 mg at bedtime to 300 mg three times a day. I'm avoiding oral steroids because his sugars are already high. Continue the metformin, lisinopril, atorvastatin, and omeprazole as they are. I'm referring him to physical therapy. He should walk short distances several times a day and avoid prolonged sitting and heavy lifting. If he is not improving in four to six weeks we'll get an MRI of the lumbar spine, sooner if he has more weakness. Go to the emergency room right away for numbness in the groin, trouble with bladder or bowels, or worsening leg weakness. And see your regular doctor about the blood sugars.
Patient: Okay.
Family member: Thank you, I'll make sure he takes the right pills.
summary: A 52-year-old male with type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and reflux had ten days of low back pain radiating down the right leg after lifting boxes, with tingling over the foot. His wife clarified that he took ibuprofen 800 mg three times a day, and that metformin is now 1000 mg twice a day. Exam showed a positive right straight leg raise, weak right big toe extension, and decreased sensation over the right foot, with mild disc space narrowing on lumbar X-ray. The assessment was right L5 lumbar radiculopathy without red flags. Ibuprofen was stopped, acetaminophen was started, gabapentin was increased to 300 mg three times a day, and physical therapy was arranged.

Telehealth visit conducted by telephone (audio only). Rheumatology follow-up for ankylosing spondylitis. The patient consented to the phone visit and was at home.

History as reported by the patient: a 25-year-old male with ankylosing spondylitis diagnosed 3 years ago, HLA-B27 positive. Over the last 3 months he has had worsening inflammatory low back pain with morning stiffness lasting about 90 minutes, pain that wakes him in the second half of the night, and buttock pain that alternates sides. He reports fatigue. His self-rated BASDAI is 6.2. He denies eye pain or redness, new rash, abdominal pain, diarrhea, fever, and peripheral joint swelling. Naproxen 500 mg twice daily for the past 4 months has only partly helped, and he previously tried celecoxib 200 mg daily for 2 months without enough benefit. He takes naproxen with food and has had no stomach upset.

Home measurements: temperature 98.2 F, BP 118/74, pulse 66 on a home cuff.

Exam: telephone only, so no physical exam. He speaks comfortably in full sentences.

Data reviewed: CRP 18 mg/L (normal below 5) and ESR 28. MRI of the sacroiliac joints 2 months ago showed active bilateral sacroiliitis with bone marrow edema. QuantiFERON-TB and hepatitis B surface antigen were negative last week.

Impression: active ankylosing spondylitis with high disease activity despite two NSAIDs.

Next steps: start secukinumab 150 mg subcutaneously weekly for 5 weeks, then every 4 weeks. Continue naproxen 500 mg twice daily with food and add omeprazole 20 mg daily for stomach protection. A nurse will teach self-injection by video. Daily stretching and a physical therapy referral. CBC and CMP in 3 months. Telephone follow-up in 12 weeks; call sooner for fever, eye redness or pain, or a severe flare.

note:
Dictating a hospital day 2 progress note on a 90-year-old male admitted with an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Overnight he had no further melena or hematemesis, no chest pain, no lightheadedness, and no abdominal pain. He has been taking over the counter naproxen for knee pain, about two tablets daily, correction, naproxen 220 mg, one tablet twice a day. He tells me he has also been skipping his omeprazole and his metoprolol for the past two months because he could not afford the copays. He also takes aspirin 81 mg daily and has a history of coronary artery disease and hypertension.

Vital signs this morning blood pressure 118/64, heart rate 84, temperature 98.4 F, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96% on room air. On admission his hemoglobin was 6.9, he received a transfusion of two units of packed red blood cells, and this morning hemoglobin is 8.5, correction, 8.6. BUN 38, creatinine 1.3, INR 1.1. The EGD yesterday showed a 1.5 centimeter duodenal bulb ulcer with a visible vessel which was treated with epinephrine injection and two hemoclips, and biopsies were taken for H pylori. On exam he is alert and comfortable, heart is regular without a murmur, abdomen is soft, nontender, and nondistended with bowel sounds present.

Assessment is acute upper gastrointestinal bleed from a duodenal bulb ulcer in the setting of naproxen use and missed omeprazole doses, with acute blood loss anemia that is improved after transfusion. Plan is to continue pantoprazole 40 mg IV twice daily for 72 hours and then transition to an oral proton pump inhibitor twice daily. Naproxen is stopped permanently. Aspirin 81 mg is held today, and we will plan to restart it in the next two to three days once hemostasis is stable. Resume metoprolol tartrate 25 mg twice daily. Advance to a soft diet today. Transfuse for hemoglobin below 7. Repeat CBC this afternoon and tomorrow morning. Follow up the H pylori biopsy results and treat if positive. Case management and pharmacy consults for medication cost assistance and low cost generic options. Anticipate discharge in one to two days.

The assessment was a duodenal bulb ulcer bleed with improving acute blood loss anemia. Pantoprazole IV was continued, naproxen was stopped, aspirin was held, metoprolol was resumed, and case management and pharmacy were consulted for cost assistance.
